Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'comments on family' is not impossible as a trigger, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear assault-linked context. The other triggers and memory items point to sensory/intrusive re-experiencing, whereas this item suggests a family-related theme not represented elsewhere in threat, appraisals, or memory.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies a bereavement/loss-focused coping target, but no other selected items indicate death loss or grief as a central aspect of the assault trauma. This maladaptive strategy does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on assault-related intrusive memory, dissociation, and social avoidance.

vignette: David spent the better part of his career listening to the quiet burdens of students, but thirty years ago, his own world fractured in the concrete shadows of a downtown parking garage. He had been leaving a neighborhood bar when a man, reeking of spilled whiskey, lunged from behind a pillar. Before David could react, heavy hands pinned his shoulders to the ground, and a fist struck his jaw repeatedly. The assault was brutal, leaving him bruised and gasping. When paramedics arrived, they loaded him into an ambulance and wheeled him into a bustling emergency department. While surgeons worked to repair a split eyebrow and a fractured wrist, the ward was saturated with the sharp, chemical bite of antiseptic cleaner, a smell that clung to the paper gown David wore and the air he kept struggling to fill his lungs. In the months that followed, David noticed how certain moments began to hijack his nervous system. At a community town hall, the custodian mopped the floors nearby; the unmistakable chemical tang of hospital-grade disinfectant drifted through the vents. Instantly, his chest tightened and the present dissolved. The room vanished, replaced by the same paralyzing terror he had felt that night, flashing through his mind in stark, frozen pictures—the concrete pressing against his back, the attacker’s shadow looming overhead. Those fragmented moments would surface unbidden, lingering for a breath before slipping away. When a committee member reached out to rest a reassuring hand on his arm, the sudden intrusion of emotional closeness sparked the exact same alarm, dragging him back to that violation. Rather than sit with the panic, David learned to manage it by withdrawing. Each time the terror rose and the snapshots returned, he would deliberately attempt to leave his body, forcing his attention inward until the world went dull. He began avoiding other people, declining invitations and convincing himself that solitude was the only way to stay safe. When his wife, Clara, tried to sit close on the couch or gently brush his shoulder, David would shift away, telling himself that being emotionally close or intimate with others was a vulnerability he could no longer afford. He was certain that if he let his guard down, the ground would give way again. Over years, these precautions hardened into routine. As a school counselor, he stopped entering the nurse’s office when students brought in scrapes, opting to handle everything from the hallway to avoid medical scents, and he trained himself to keep conversations strictly professional, deflecting any personal connection. The distance David built around himself, however, only trained his mind to scan for threats. By deliberately blanking out during early signs of distress and pushing away anyone who drew near, he reinforced the unspoken rule that proximity was dangerous. Consequently, normal social gestures became magnified warning signs. A colleague leaning in to share a file felt like an encroachment, and the faint trace of alcohol from a parent’s coat at pickup hours triggered the same hypervigilant scanning. His avoidance strategies had narrowed his world so thoroughly that his nervous system remained locked in anticipatory dread, where every unfamiliar scent or overture felt like the opening frame of a nightmare he was still trapped inside. At sixty-eight, David now sits in his third-floor office, staring at an annual safety checklist he can no longer complete. He has missed three staff training sessions this month, claiming migraines, and has begun leaving early to avoid the evening commutes past the clinic downtown. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that he was no longer counseling anyone; he was merely waiting for the next blow to land. He is terrified that his carefully constructed walls have become a cage, leaving him completely alone with the echoes of a night that ended decades ago. He hopes, though he does not know how, to find a way to breathe through the antiseptic, to let someone sit beside him without flinching, and to finally step out of the garage.
